Note: Corippus explicitly describes Gurzil as the son of Ammon and a cow. This provides a direct familial connection in the surviving late-antique account, although it does not establish how early or widely this genealogy was accepted in indigenous Libyan religion.

The Carthaginian tophet inscriptions repeatedly invoke Tanit, commonly alongside Baal Hammon, in votive formulas recording that an offering was made in fulfillment of a vow and that the deity heard and blessed the dedicator. This corpus provides the strongest direct epigraphic evidence for Tanit’s central place in Punic ritual.

The twenty-eight-book Carthaginian Agricultural Treatise is attributed to Mago. After the fall of Carthage, the Roman Senate ordered it translated into Latin, and later Greek and Roman agricultural writers preserved fragments and adaptations of its contents.

Jugurtha was Masinissa’s biological grandson through Masinissa’s son Mastanabal. He was subsequently raised and adopted by his uncle Micipsa, which placed him within the ruling household alongside Micipsa’s sons Adherbal and Hiempsal.

Masinissa began the Second Punic War aligned with Carthage but later joined Scipio. At the Battle of Zama in 202 BCE, his Numidian cavalry fought against Hannibal’s army, drove off the Carthaginian cavalry, and returned to strike Hannibal’s infantry from the rear, contributing decisively to the Roman victory.
